Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- A crowd of about 10,000 came to Dodger Stadium on Saturday, but they weren't there for a baseball game. Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez from L.A. County Probation Department. While the Dodgers were in Arizona for spring training, more than 80 employers set up employment booths in the parking lot just beyond the center field fence. To those who turned out, finding a job would be a home run. Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe's and Union Bank. And government agencies including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers  were there, too. All had one thing in common: They were hiring. And that was music to the ears of 30-year-old Eric Clardy. It has been a rough couple of years for Clardy. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market started to tank. Then, after finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, layoffs struck again. "It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want," he said. Clardy said his goal is to make contact with at least 10 potential employers a day via phone, letters and the Internet. Being unemployed is hard work, too.  Watch how Clardy goes about trying to find a job » . "It was a scramble," Clardy said. "I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs." The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday's event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair to fill some 500 part-time jobs at the stadium during baseball season drew about 7,000 applicants. California's unemployment rate is 10.1 percent, a full 2 percentage points higher than the national rate. The state's Employment Development office estimates that nearly a half-million state residents have lost their jobs in the past year. "We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she said, "There are jobs available." But at Dodger Stadium, it was clear that competition for those available jobs is stiff. Applicants were often stacked four and five people deep in front of employer tables, and there was little chance for most of the 10,000 job seekers to make much of an impression. But organizers worked hard to pump up any flagging spirits. "Yes we can. Yes we can," Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker. State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they are among the nation's hardest-hit in this economic downturn, but he exhorted them to not give up. "We will get out of this economic funk," he said. "We will recover soon. We've got to have hope." Garcia and deLeon's comments echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently won approval of a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package. Recruiters from the government agencies present at the job fair said that money will start creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants that it is hiring for a wide variety of positions, including those for engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers. The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation of the 2010 census, and other federal agencies are hiring as well. All of that was good news to Clardy, who left resumes and filled out applications at a number of the 80 booths cluttering the stadium's parking lot. But he remained realistic about this day's activities leading directly to a job. "It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," he said. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore."

Keywords: LOS, ANGELES, California

outputs.L1:
**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)** — About 10,000 people gathered at Dodger Stadium on Saturday—but they were not there for a baseball game.

*Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez of the L.A. County Probation Department.*

While the Dodgers were in Arizona for spring training, more than 80 employers set up recruitment booths in the parking lot just beyond the center-field fence. For those who attended, finding a job would have been a home run.

Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe’s and Union Bank. Government agencies—including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers—were also represented.

They all had one thing in common: They were hiring.

That was music to the ears of 30-year-old Eric Clardy, who has endured a difficult couple of years. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market began to collapse. After finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, he was hit by layoffs again.

“It’s kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want,” he said.

Clardy said his goal is to contact at least 10 potential employers each day by phone, letter and the Internet. Being unemployed, he has found, is hard work, too.

*Watch how Clardy goes about trying to find a job »*

“It was a scramble,” Clardy said. “I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs.”

The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday’s event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair aimed at filling approximately 500 part-time stadium jobs during baseball season attracted about 7,000 applicants.

California’s unemployment rate is 10.1 percent—a full 2 percentage points above the national rate. The state’s Employment Development office estimates that nearly half a million California residents have lost their jobs over the past year.

“We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago,” said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles.

Nonetheless, she said, “There are jobs available.”

At Dodger Stadium, however, it was clear that competition for those jobs was fierce. Applicants often stood four or five deep in front of employers’ tables, leaving most of the 10,000 job seekers with little opportunity to make a strong impression.

Organizers nevertheless worked hard to lift flagging spirits.

“Yes we can. Yes we can,” Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker.

State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they were among those hardest hit by the nation’s economic downturn, but he urged them not to give up.

“We will get out of this economic funk,” he said. “We will recover soon. We’ve got to have hope.”

Garcia’s and deLeon’s remarks echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently secured approval for a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package.

Recruiters from government agencies represented at the job fair said the funding would begin creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants that it was hiring for a wide range of positions, including engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers.

The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation for the 2010 census, while other federal agencies are hiring as well.

All of this was welcome news to Clardy, who left résumés and completed applications at several of the 80 booths filling the stadium parking lot. Still, he remained realistic about the likelihood that the day’s efforts would lead directly to a job.

“It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview,” he said. “Now it doesn’t seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore.”

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Roughly 10,000 people gathered at Dodger Stadium on Saturday for an event unrelated to baseball. Among them was job hunter Eric Clardy, pictured greeting Raul Mendez, a recruiter with the Los Angeles County Probation Department.

With the Dodgers away at spring training in Arizona, the parking area beyond the center-field wall was transformed into a hiring fair featuring more than 80 employers. For those attending, landing a position would have felt like hitting a home run.

Businesses such as Coca-Cola, Lowe’s and Union Bank took part, alongside public agencies including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers. Every participating organization shared one important feature: available jobs.

That was welcome news for Clardy, 30, who had endured two difficult years. He first lost his position as a loan processor when the housing market began collapsing. He later secured work as a project manager at a plumbing company, only to be laid off again.

Clardy said his immediate priority was finding employment to cover his expenses, after which he could focus on building the career he ultimately wanted. He aimed to contact at least 10 prospective employers each day by telephone, mail or online. His experience showed that searching for work could itself be demanding.

He described the period as a frantic struggle in which he sold insurance, accepted temporary assignments and attended employment fairs.

Saturday’s event was arranged by the city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department, whose officials estimated attendance at about 10,000. Earlier in the same month, approximately 7,000 people had applied during a two-day fair seeking to fill around 500 part-time, seasonal positions at the stadium.

California’s jobless rate stood at 10.1 percent—two percentage points above the nationwide figure. The state Employment Development Department estimated that close to 500,000 Californians had become unemployed during the previous year.

Gloria Bratton Moore, who manages the publicly funded Work Source employment center in Los Angeles, said job openings were less plentiful than they had been one year earlier. Even so, she emphasized that positions could still be found.

The scene at Dodger Stadium demonstrated how intense the competition was. At many recruiters’ tables, applicants formed crowds four or five rows deep, leaving most of the approximately 10,000 attendees with little opportunity to distinguish themselves.

Organizers nevertheless tried to keep morale high. Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia repeatedly led the crowd in the “Yes we can” chant over a loudspeaker. California legislator Kevin deLeon told participants that they were among those most severely affected by the national economic decline, while urging them to remain optimistic. He predicted that the economy would emerge from its slump and recover soon, stressing the importance of hope.

Their remarks recalled themes from President Obama’s campaign. Obama had recently secured approval for an economic recovery package worth almost $800 billion.

Representatives of government agencies at the fair said the stimulus funding would begin generating employment within several months. The Army Corps of Engineers announced openings across numerous fields, including engineering, heavy-machinery operation and environmental fieldwork. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department was preparing to add more than 1 million positions for the 2010 census, and other federal departments were also recruiting.

Clardy welcomed those developments. He submitted applications and left copies of his résumé at several of the 80 booths filling the stadium parking lot. Still, he did not assume that the day’s efforts would immediately produce a job.

He observed that, only a few years earlier, attending a career fair often functioned much like an initial interview. By then, however, that no longer appeared to be the case, and some employers were not even accepting résumés at such events.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a massive job fair at Dodger Stadium during the recession, focusing on unemployed job seeker Eric Clardy and California’s 10.1 percent unemployment rate.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thousands flock to Dodger Stadium as California unemployment hits 10.1%**

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Dodger Stadium is accustomed to crowds, long lines and anxious fans. But during a massive job fair held amid the recession, the prize was not a baseball victory. It was a paycheck.

Thousands of unemployed and underemployed Californians streamed into the stadium carrying résumés and hoping to meet employers. Among them was Eric Clardy, a job seeker confronting the same difficult market as hundreds of thousands of other state residents.

Clardy moved through the fair looking for an opportunity — any promising lead in an economy where openings had become scarce and competition intense. Around him, applicants waited to speak with recruiters representing companies in fields ranging from retail and health care to finance and public service.

The turnout offered a stark picture of California’s economic pain. The state’s unemployment rate had climbed to 10.1%, as employers cut jobs and consumers reduced spending. California’s housing collapse and exposure to struggling construction, real estate and financial industries made the downturn especially severe.

For Clardy, the statistics were personal. Finding work meant navigating crowded aisles, making quick introductions and trying to stand out among a sea of qualified applicants.

Job fairs can provide face-to-face access that online applications cannot, but they also demonstrate how dramatically the balance has shifted toward employers. Recruiters who once struggled to fill positions were now able to choose from large pools of candidates, many with years of experience.

Outside the stadium, lines formed early as applicants arrived dressed for interviews and carrying folders of résumés. Some had been unemployed for months. Others feared their current jobs might soon disappear.

California officials faced growing pressure to respond as unemployment offices dealt with rising claims and families struggled to cover mortgages, rent and health care. Economists warned that even after the broader economy began to recover, hiring could remain weak for months.

Inside Dodger Stadium, however, job seekers focused less on forecasts than on the next handshake.

For Clardy and thousands like him, the massive gathering represented both the depth of the recession and a measure of hope: the possibility that one conversation might lead to an interview — and, eventually, a job.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news report on the roughly 10,000 people who attended a Los Angeles job fair featuring more than 80 employers, including government agencies and major companies.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nearly 10,000 job seekers crowd Los Angeles hiring fair

**LOS ANGELES —** Roughly 10,000 people attended a large Los Angeles job fair featuring more than 80 employers, underscoring the intense demand for work across Southern California.

Government agencies and major private-sector companies sent recruiters to meet applicants, explain available positions and, in some cases, begin the screening process. The openings represented a broad range of fields, including public safety, transportation, health care, logistics, retail, hospitality, administration and skilled trades.

Long lines formed as job seekers arrived with résumés and moved among employer booths. Some participants were looking for their first full-time jobs, while others said they were trying to reenter the workforce, change careers or find more stable employment after layoffs and reduced hours.

Recruiters used the event to promote both entry-level and experienced positions. Government representatives also provided information about civil-service examinations, background checks and application procedures—steps that can make public-sector hiring more complicated and time-consuming than applying for many private-sector jobs.

The attendance figure, estimated at about 10,000, highlighted the mismatch between the number of people seeking work and the number of opportunities immediately available. Although more than 80 employers participated, the event did not guarantee jobs to attendees. Applicants were generally encouraged to submit online applications, follow up with recruiters and prepare for interviews or additional assessments.

For employers, the fair offered access to a large and diverse pool of candidates in a single day. Public agencies have been working to fill vacancies created by retirements and persistent staffing shortages, while major companies continue to recruit for positions with varying education and experience requirements.

The turnout also reflected broader concerns about the cost of living in Los Angeles. High housing, food and transportation expenses have increased the pressure on residents to secure dependable work, higher wages and benefits. For many attendees, health insurance, retirement plans and predictable schedules were as important as starting pay.

Job fairs can help applicants make direct contact with recruiters, but employment specialists caution that they are usually only the beginning of the hiring process. Candidates are advised to tailor their résumés, complete required applications promptly and maintain contact with employers after the event.

No immediate total was available for the number of interviews, conditional offers or eventual hires resulting from the fair. Organizers and participating employers were expected to continue reviewing applications after the event.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a 2009 CNN article describing fierce competition among job seekers at Dodger Stadium and the hope that the federal economic stimulus package will create new employment opportunities.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thousands crowd Dodger Stadium in search of work**

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) —** The competition at Dodger Stadium on Thursday was not for a place in the starting lineup. It was for a paycheck.

Thousands of job seekers filled the stadium’s parking lots for a sprawling employment fair, many arriving hours before the gates opened. Applicants in business suits stood shoulder to shoulder, clutching résumés and waiting for brief conversations with recruiters.

Some had been unemployed for months. Others still had jobs but feared they could be next as companies continued to cut payrolls amid the deepening recession.

“I’ve sent out dozens of applications and barely received a response,” said one applicant, a former office manager. “You come here and realize everyone is competing for the same few openings.”

The scene reflected a rapidly deteriorating labor market. The national unemployment rate reached 8.1 percent in February, and employers eliminated more than 650,000 jobs during the month. California’s housing collapse and budget problems have added to the strain.

Recruiters at the stadium said openings were available in health care, sales, transportation, public safety and other fields. But with long lines forming at nearly every booth, applicants knew that an introduction and a résumé might not be enough.

Many pinned their hopes on the $787 billion federal economic stimulus package signed by President Obama in February. The measure includes spending on roads, schools, energy projects and public services, as well as tax relief intended to encourage consumer spending and business investment.

Administration officials say the package will create or preserve millions of jobs. Economists caution that the effect will take time and that unemployment may continue rising before stimulus-funded projects begin hiring.

For those searching at Dodger Stadium, however, even the possibility of new work offered a measure of hope.

“People want to work,” another job seeker said as he moved toward the next recruiter’s table. “We’re just waiting for someone to give us a chance.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Eric Clardy’s search for work after being laid off twice, using the Dodger Stadium employment fair as the backdrop and including quotes from organizers, officials, and recruiters.
counterfactuals.output:
LOS ANGELES — For Eric Clardy, the employment fair at Dodger Stadium was another stop in a job search made urgent by two layoffs. After finding work following his first dismissal, he was laid off again, sending him back into a crowded labor market and forcing him to compete with thousands of other applicants.

Clardy arrived at the stadium carrying résumés and hoping that face-to-face contact with employers would produce what online applications had not. “I’ve been laid off twice,” he said, describing the second setback as especially discouraging. Still, he viewed the fair as a chance to meet recruiters directly rather than remain one more name in an electronic queue.

The ballpark’s parking areas and concourses, normally filled with baseball fans, became rows of employer booths. Organizers said the heavy turnout illustrated both the depth of unemployment in Los Angeles and the determination of people trying to return to work. They described the fair as a way to bring job seekers together with employers that had actual openings, not merely information about possible future hiring.

Public officials at the event acknowledged that a job fair could not solve the region’s unemployment problem. But they said it could connect residents with immediate opportunities and with training, résumé assistance and other services. The central message, one official said, was that job seekers “should not give up,” even after months of rejection.

Recruiters said candidates needed to be flexible. Employers were looking for people who could demonstrate transferable skills, communicate clearly and accept work outside their previous industries. One recruiter advised applicants to “keep an open mind,” while another stressed that a résumé alone was not enough: candidates had to explain how their experience could meet an employer’s current needs.

For Clardy, the fair offered no guarantee of a job. Its value was the possibility of making a personal impression and finding a lead after the repeated disruption of being laid off. As he moved from booth to booth, his experience reflected the larger scene at Dodger Stadium: thousands of people hoping that a brief conversation with a recruiter might become a route back to steady work.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# Job Seekers Come to Dodger Stadium Hoping to Hit a Home Run

**LOS ANGELES —** Dodger Stadium became a field of opportunity as job seekers arrived carrying résumés instead of baseball gloves, hoping that conversations with employers would lead to their next career.

The stadium job fair brought together private companies, government agencies and military recruiters at a time when many Southern California residents were searching for steady work. Attendees moved among booths staffed by representatives from major employers, including **Coca-Cola, Lowe’s and Union Bank**, asking about openings, qualifications and the application process.

Public-sector organizations also attracted considerable interest. Recruiters from the **FBI** spoke with applicants about careers in law enforcement, intelligence, technology and administration, while the **Army Corps of Engineers** highlighted opportunities in engineering, construction and other technical fields.

Another potential source of work was the upcoming **2010 census**. Census recruiters promoted temporary positions needed to help count residents across the region, offering job seekers a chance to earn income while supporting the once-a-decade national effort.

For many attendees, the appeal of the event was the opportunity to meet employers face to face rather than submit another online application. Some came looking for an immediate paycheck; others hoped to change careers or find work with better pay and benefits.

The baseball setting supplied an easy metaphor for the day. Not every conversation would result in an offer, but job seekers came prepared to take a swing — and, if possible, leave Dodger Stadium having hit a professional home run.
